title: VoltStream: EV Charger Data Check
subtitle: An AI assistant that knows when to ask for help

slides.eyebrow: Con Edison EV charger data · Capstone project
slides.title: When charger records disagree, should AI choose a number?
slides.lead: Con Edison receives charger information through outside contractors and data companies. Those submissions can use different formats, names, and values.
slides.boundary: We built and tested a small AI assistant that organizes each submission, checks for problems, and knows when a person must decide.

slides.title: A simple data-entry task becomes difficult when files disagree
slides.lead: A contractor may send a spreadsheet, an API record, or a note. The same charger can be described differently—or have important information missing.
leftItems: Different column names and file formats
rightItems: Where did that value come from?
Is the record ready, or must someone review it?
slides.note: Our project focuses only on this first check. We did not use Con Edison internal data or claim measured labor savings.

slides.title: Mixed data is normal—even in a national charger directory
slides.fact: The U.S. Department of Energy's charging-station directory combines daily network feeds, spreadsheet/CSV imports, and records maintained by people.
slides.implication: A useful system must show what it knows, what it does not know, and which original field supports each answer. A complete-looking row is not enough.
slides.sources: Sources: DOE Alternative Fuels Data Center; NREL developer documentation; Con Edison PowerReady; NYSDPS Case 18-E-0138.

slides.eyebrow: 03 · How we chose the project scope
slides.title: We chose the smallest useful part of a much larger problem

choices.name: Let AI freely rewrite the data
choices.description: The output looked convincing, but it was hard to see when the AI had guessed.

choices.name: Build the entire company data platform
choices.description: Useful as a long-term idea, but too large to build and test honestly in this project.

choices.name: Check each new submission
choices.description: Put incoming data into one format, flag problems, and send uncertain cases to a person.

slides.note: The prototype answers one question: what should happen to this submission before anyone relies on it?

slides.title: The prototype does four simple things

steps.title: Organize
steps.detail: Place the facts into the same 8 boxes

steps.title: Check
steps.detail: Find missing, invalid, or conflicting values

steps.title: Decide
steps.detail: Ready · ask a person · cannot use

slides.guardrail: The AI suggests the values. Regular code applies the safety rules and makes the final decision.
slides.excluded: The 8 boxes are station ID, address, charger level, port count, power, plug type, operating status, and the original record ID.

slides.eyebrow: 04 · What failed and what we changed
slides.title: Our first idea was too confident when the data was unclear
slides.primary: The free-form AI cleaner saw two different port counts, chose 8, and marked the record ready. We stopped using that approach as the default.

events.label: Test setup 1
events.detail: A nested JSON example broke the prompt template. We fixed it and added a test so it could not return.

events.label: Test setup 2
events.detail: One output rule was not supported by Codex. We simplified the rule and tested the new version.

events.label: Discarded run
events.detail: A status check finished before the final files were written. We corrected the record and excluded that run from the comparison.

slides.boundary: The discarded run was a testing-process problem, not a model failure. Only the later frozen run is used as evidence.

slides.eyebrow: 04 · The case that changed our decision
slides.title: If one file says 8 and 6, the AI must not guess
slides.takeaway: The four DeepSeek approaches were right on at least 95% of individual fields, but this one unsafe approval was enough to reject them for automation.

slides.title: The next improvement is a better conflict check—not a bigger model

signals.title: Codex with safety rules
signals.description: Its one decision error was cautious: it sent a usable text case for extra review instead of approving it.

signals.title: DeepSeek Pro
signals.description: It was good at showing where values came from, but it still made the unsafe choice in the 8-versus-6 case.

slides.next: Add a rule that detects competing numbers in the original file, improve source tracking for text, then test many more unseen cases.

slides.title: We wrote the correct answers before asking any AI system
slides.method: The 10 examples were made for this test; no company records were used. We fixed the answer sheet, scoring rules, and AI instructions before the final run.
slides.gate: Automatic rejection from the pilot: any unsafe approval, invented critical value, or failure to resist the malicious instruction.

slides.title: Only one AI approach was accurate and made no unsafe approval
slides.note: Codex and DeepSeek are two families of generative AI models. “Sources right” means the answer points back to the correct original field. “Veto” means one unsafe result disqualified the approach.

slides.title: The cheaper approaches still failed the safety test
findings: Using rules first avoided only 1 of 10 model calls—about 10%, below our 40% target.
Pro cost about 3.15× as much as protected Flash and still made the unsafe choice.
Codex was slower. A comparable price was unavailable, so we do not claim it was cost-effective.

slides.title: Use it as an assistant, never as the final decision-maker
slides.decision: The evidence supports a limited, fully human-reviewed pilot of Codex with safety rules. It does not support production deployment; a person must review every suggested record.
guardrails: Use only approved test data and keep the original file
Show exactly where every suggested value came from
Do not let the tool update an official system
Stop the trial after any invented critical value or unsafe approval
beforeExpansion: Improve source tracking in written notes
Test a larger set labeled by independent reviewers

slides.eyebrow: 08 · What we still do not know
slides.title: Ten made-up examples cannot prove this will work in daily operations

risks.title: Models change
risks.detail: A provider update could change the answers.

risks.title: People may trust it too much
risks.detail: A neat-looking result can still be wrong.

risks.title: Real files may be different
risks.detail: New formats and multi-row files remain untested.

risks.title: Privacy is unresolved
risks.detail: We have not reviewed how real company data should be handled.

risks.title: Human workload is unknown
risks.detail: We have not measured review time at scale.

risks.title: Eight boxes may be too simple
risks.detail: Real business data may need more distinctions.

slides.nextGate: Before any wider use: repeat the test, have two people label the answers, review privacy, measure review time, and define when to roll back.
slides.close: The evidence supports a careful next experiment—not automation.
